Introduction to Graph.theory: A graph consists of vertices and edges, directed or undirected, weighted or unweighted. These lessons use zero-based vertices. Adjacency lists use O(V+E) memory; matrices use O(V²). An undirected edge normally occurs in both adjacency lists. A traversal must restart from every unvisited vertex to cover disconnected components. BFS gives shortest edge distance in unweighted graphs; DFS explores reachability. Weighted shortest paths need algorithms selected by edge constraints: Dijkstra for nonnegative weights, DAG order for acyclic graphs, Bellman-Ford when negative weights occur. Cycles mean a visited structure is essential; do not apply tree traversal assumptions.

Traversal Techniques.complexity: O(V+E) time and O(V+E) input/working storage; recursive DFS can use O(V) call stack.

MST theory.theory: A spanning tree connects all V vertices using V-1 edges and no cycle. An MST minimizes total weight. If the graph is disconnected there is no spanning tree; algorithms may instead return a minimum spanning forest. Cut property: a minimum-weight edge across any cut can be included in an MST, because exchanging it for the edge an MST uses across that cut cannot increase weight. Kruskal sorts edges and accepts ones connecting separate components (DSU). Prim repeatedly adds the smallest edge connecting the built tree to an outside vertex. Negative edge weights are fine for MST. Directed graphs require different arborescence algorithms.
